name: Independent Set
description: Eric is the teacher of graph theory class. Today, Eric teaches independent set and edge-induced subgraph. Given a graph $$$G=(V,E)$$$, an independent set is a subset of vertices $$$V' \subset V$$$ such that for every pair $$$u,v \in V'$$$, $$$(u,v) \not \in E$$$ (i.e. no edge in $$$E$$$ connects two vertices from $$$V'$$$). An edge-induced subgraph consists of a subset of edges $$$E' \subset E$$$ and all the vertices in the original graph that are incident on at least one edge in the subgraph. Given $$$E' \subset E$$$, denote $$$G[E']$$$ the edge-induced subgraph such that $$$E'$$$ is the edge set of the subgraph. Here is an illustration of those definitions: In order to help his students get familiar with those definitions, he leaves the following problem as an exercise: Given a tree $$$G=(V,E)$$$, calculate the sum of $$$w(H)$$$ over all except null edge-induced subgraph $$$H$$$ of $$$G$$$, where $$$w(H)$$$ is the number of independent sets in $$$H$$$. Formally, calculate $$$\sum \limits_{\emptyset \not= E' \subset E} w(G[E'])$$$. Show Eric that you are smarter than his students by providing the correct answer as quickly as possible. Note that the answer might be large, you should output the answer modulo $$$998,244,353$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^5$$$), representing the number of vertices of the graph $$$G$$$. Each of the following $$$n-1$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u,v \le n$$$, $$$u \not= v$$$), describing edges of the given tree. It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree.
output_specification: Output one integer, representing the desired value modulo $$$998,244,353$$$.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1332F — Independent Set [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
